'''Thomas Eugene Everhart''' [[FREng]] (born February 15, 1932, in [[Kansas City, Missouri]])<ref name=OralHistoryCHF>{{cite book|last1= Brock |first1=David C.|first2=Cyrus |last2=Mody|title=Thomas E. Everhart, Transcript of an Interview Conducted by David C. Brock and Cyrus Mody as a phone interview and in Santa Barbara, California on 28 March 2007 and 3 May 2011 |date=3 May 2011 |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/sites/default/files/interview_pdf_abstract/everhart_te_0689_suppl.pdf|place=Philadelphia, PA|publisher=[[Chemical Heritage Foundation]] }}</ref> is an American university president, educator, and [[physicist]]. His area of expertise is the physics of [[electron]] beams.  Together with [[Richard F. M. Thornley]] he designed the [[Everhart–Thornley detector]]. These detectors are still in use in [[scanning electron microscope]]s, even though the first such detector was made available as early as 1956.

Everhart was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 1978 for contributions to the electron optics of the scanning electron microscope and to its use in electronics and biology. He was appointed an International [[Fellow]] of the [[Royal Academy of Engineering]] in 1990.<ref name=Fellows>{{cite web|title=List of Fellows|url=http://www.raeng.org.uk/about-us/people-council-committees/the-fellowship/list-of-fellows?fa=e&p=2|website=Royal Academy of Engineering}}</ref> He served as chancellor of the [[University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign]] from  1984 to 1987 and as the president of the [[California Institute of Technology]] from 1987 to 1997.

== Early life and education==
Everhart's parents were William E. Everhart and Elizabeth A. West. Everhart received his [[A.B.]] in physics from [[Harvard University]] in 1953, and his [[M.S.]] in applied physics from the [[University of California, Los Angeles]], in 1955.  He held a [[Marshall Scholarship]] at [[Clare College, Cambridge]], where he completed a PhD in physics under Professor [[Charles Oatley]] in 1958.<ref name=OralHistoryCHF/>

==Career==

=== Everhart-Thornley detector ===

Everhart began working on electron detection and the design of [[scanning electron microscopes]] (SEMs) as a student with Charles Oatley at Cambridge in 1955.<ref name=Rodenburg>{{cite book|last1=Rodenburg|first1=J.M.|authorlink1=John Rodenburg|title=Electron microscopy and analysis 1997 : proceedings of the Institute of Physics Electron Microscopy and Analysis Group conference, Cavendish Laboratory, University of Cambridge, 2-5 September 1997|date=1997|publisher=Institute of Physics Pub.|location=Bristol|isbn=978-0750304412|pages=11–16|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tN-4AwLMr0EC&pg=PA11|accessdate=19 June 2015}}</ref> An initial prototype, the SEM1, had been developed by Dennis McMullen, who published his dissertation ''Investigations relating to the design of electron microscopes'' in 1952.<ref name=Rodenburg/><ref name=Ratinac/> It was further modified by Ken C. A. Smith, who developed a way to efficiently detect low-energy secondary electrons.<ref name=Chapter>{{cite book|last=Everhart|first=T. E. | chapter= Contrast formation in the scanning electron microscope|pages=137–145| editor-last1=Hawkes|editor-first1=Peter W.|title=Advances in imaging and electron physics: Volume 133, Sir Charles Oatley and the Scanning Electron Microscope|date=2004|publisher=Elsevier Academic Press|location=Oxford|isbn=978-0123859853|edition=1st|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UaWPclp1K2QC&pg=PA202}}</ref> Oatley and his students used SEM to develop a variety of new techniques for studying surface topography.<ref name=Rodenburg /><ref name=Holt>{{cite book|last1=Holt|first1=D. B.|last2=Joy|first2=D. C.|title=SEM Microcharacterization of Semiconductors|date=1989|publisher=Elsevier Science|isbn=9780123538550|pages=xi–xii|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=w81GBQAAQBAJ&pg=PR11|accessdate=18 June 2015}}</ref>

Everhart developed techniques to detect low-energy secondaries. His Ph.D. thesis, in 1958, was ''Contrast formation in the scanning electron microscope''.<ref name=Holt/> Analyzing the electrons detected by the SEM, he reported that about 67% of the signal measured could be attributed to low energy secondaries from the specimen.<ref name=Hawkes/> About 3% was due to higher-energy reflected electrons.<ref name=Chapter/> He also presented equations to model the noise introduced.<ref name=Rodenburg/><ref name=Hawkes>{{cite book|last1=Hawkes|first1=Peter W.|title=Advances in imaging and electron physics: Volume 133, Sir Charles Oatley and the Scanning Electron Microscope|date=2004|publisher=Elsevier Academic Press|location=Oxford|isbn=978-0123859853|edition=1st|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UaWPclp1K2QC&pg=PA202}}</ref>

Use of the term "voltage contrast" to describe the relationship between the voltage applied to a specimen and the resulting image contrast, is attributed to Everhart.<ref name=Breton>{{cite web|last1=Breton|first1=Bernie C.|title=The Early History and Development of The Scanning Electron Microscope|url=http://www-g.eng.cam.ac.uk/125/achievements/oatley/history.html|website=University of Cambridge|accessdate=18 June 2015}}</ref><ref name=Oatley>{{cite journal|last1=Oatley|first1=CW|last2=Everhart|first2=TE|title=The examination of p-n junctions in the scanning electron microscope|journal=Journal of Electronics|date=1957|volume=2|issue=6|pages=568–570|doi=10.1080/00207215708937060}}</ref> As of 1959, Everhart produced the first voltage-contrast images of p-n junctions of biased silicon diodes.<ref name=Everhart1959>{{cite journal|last1=Everhart|first1=T.E.|last2=Wells|first2=O.C.|last3=Oatley|first3=C.W.|title=Factors affecting contrast and resolution in the scanning electron microscope|journal=Journal of Electronics Control|date=1959|volume=7|issue=2|pages=97–111|doi=10.1080/00207215908937191}}</ref> Voltage contrast, the ability to detect variations in surface electrical potentials on a specimen, is now one of several imaging modes used for the characterization, diagnosis and failure analysis of semiconductors. As many as half of the SEMs sold are believed to be used in semiconductor applications.<ref name=Newbury>{{cite book|last1=Newbury
  |first1=Dale D.
  |last2=Joy
  |first2=David C.
  |last3=Echlin
  |first3=Patrick
  |last4=Fiori
  |first4=Charles E.
  |last5=Goldstein
  |first5=Joseph I.
  |title=Advanced scanning electron microscopy and x-ray analysis
  |date=1986
  |publisher=Plenum Press, Inc.
  |location=New York
  |isbn=9780306421402
  |page=45}}</ref>

Everhart studied contrast mechanisms in detail and developed a new theory of reflection of electrons from solids.<ref name=Everhart1960>{{cite journal|last1=Everhart|first1=T. E.|title=Simple Theory Concerning the Reflection of Electrons from Solids|journal=Journal of Applied Physics|date=1960|volume=31|issue=8|pages=1483–1490|doi=10.1063/1.1735868|bibcode = 1960JAP....31.1483E }}</ref> He also made some of the first quantitative studies of the effects of beam penetration on image formation in the SEM.

In 1960 Everhart and Richard F. M. Thornley published a description for the improved design of a secondary electron detector, since known as the [[Everhart–Thornley detector]]. Everhart and Thornley increased the efficiency of existing detectors by adding a light pipe to carry the photon signal from the scintillator inside the evacuated specimen chamber of the scanning electron microscopes to the photomultiplier outside the chamber.<ref name=Detector>{{cite journal
 | author =  Everhart, TE and RFM Thornley
 | year = 1960
 | title = Wide-band detector for micro-microampere low-energy electron currents
 | journal = Journal of Scientific Instruments
 | volume = 37
 | issue = 7
 | pages = 246–248
 | doi = 10.1088/0950-7671/37/7/307
 | bibcode=1960JScI...37..246E
 | url = https://authors.library.caltech.edu/12086/1/EVEjsi60.pdf
 }}</ref>  This strengthened the signal collected and improved the signal-to-noise ratio. In 1963, Pease and Nixon incorporated the Everhart-Thornley detector into their prototype for the first commercial SEM, later developed as the [[Cambridge Scientific Instruments]] Mark I  ''Stereoscan''. This type of secondary electron and back-scattered electron detector is still used in modern [[scanning electron microscopes]] (SEMs).<ref name=Bogner>{{cite journal|last1=Bogner|first1=A.|last2=Jouneau|first2=P.-H.|last3=Thollet|first3=G.|last4=Basset|first4=D.|last5=Gauthier|first5=C.|title=A history of scanning electron microscopy developments: Towards "wet-STEM" imaging|journal=Micron|date=2007|volume=38|issue=4|pages=390–401|doi=10.1016/j.micron.2006.06.008|pmid=16990007|url=http://www.physics.emory.edu/faculty/weeks//lab/papers/bogner-micron07.pdf|accessdate=18 June 2015}}</ref>

By using various types of detectors with SEM, it becomes possible to map the topography, crystallography and composition of specimens being examined.<ref name=Ratinac>{{cite book
  |editor-last1=Ratinac
  |editor-first1=Kyle R.
  |title=50 great moments : celebrating the golden jubilee of the University of Sydney's Electron Microscope Unit
  |chapter=Great moment 9: Scanning electron microscopy
  |last1=Ratinac
  |first1=Kyle R.
  |date=2008
  |publisher=Sydney University Press
  |location=University of Sydney, N.S.W.
  |isbn=9781920898762
  |pages=71–81
  |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Okm7zPWnsvIC&pg=PA73
  |accessdate=19 June 2015}}</ref> In the 1960s, Wells, Everhart, and Matta built an advanced SEM for semiconductor studies and microfabrication at Westinghouse Laboratories in Pittsburgh. They were able to combine signals so to more effectively examine multiple layers in active devices, an early example of EBIC imaging.<ref name=Wells1965>{{cite journal|last1=Wells|first1=OC|last2=Everhart|first2=TE|last3=Matta|first3=RK|title=Automatic positioning of device electrodes using the scanning electron microscope|journal=IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices|date=1965|volume=ED-12|issue=10|pages=556–563|doi=10.1109/t-ed.1965.15607|bibcode=1965ITED...12..556W}}</ref><ref name=Everhart1971>{{cite journal|last1=Everhart|first1=T. E.|last2=Hoff|first2=P. H.|title=Determination of Kilovolt Electron Energy Dissipation vs Penetration Distance in Solid Materials|journal=Journal of Applied Physics|date=1971|volume=42|issue=13|pages=5837–5846|doi=10.1063/1.1660019|bibcode=1971JAP....42.5837E}}</ref>

===University of California, Berkeley ===
From 1958-1978 Everhart was a professor and later department chairman of electrical engineering and computer science (EECS), at the [[University of California at Berkeley]].<ref name=OralHistoryCHF/>  There he supported the construction of the first scanning electron microscope in a U.S. university.<ref>{{cite web|title=IEEE Founders Medal Recipients|website=[[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]] (IEEE) |url=http://www.ieee.org/about/awards/bios/founders_recipients.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100408000305/http://www.ieee.org/about/awards/bios/founders_recipients.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 8, 2010}}</ref>

=== Cornell University ===
In January 1979, he became Joseph Silbert Dean of the college of engineering at [[Cornell University]], Ithaca, New York.<ref name=Kavli/>

===University of Illinois ===
Everhart served as chancellor of the [[University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign]] from  1984 to 1987. As chancellor, Everhart was involved in proposals for and development of the [[Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology]], an interdisciplinary research institute substantially funded by an appeal to [[Arnold Orville Beckman]].<ref name=Brown2009>{{cite book|last1=Brown|first1=Theodore L.|title=Bridging divides : the origins of the Beckman Institute at Illinois|date=2009|publisher=University of Illinois|location=Urbana|isbn=978-0252034848|url=http://www.press.uillinois.edu/books/catalog/38tnd6hm9780252034848.html|accessdate=11 December 2014}}</ref>{{rp|9–14}} In a formal invitation to proposed members of the Administrative Committee for the Beckman Institute, Everhart wrote that creation of the Beckman Institute was "an exceptional opportunity, perhaps the most dramatic and exciting one that we will see in our working lifetimes."<ref name=Brown2009/>{{rp|97}}

===California Institute of Technology ===
Everhart was president of the [[California Institute of Technology]] from 1987 to 1997.<ref name=Woo>{{cite news|last1=Woo|first1=Elaine|title=President of Caltech Announces Resignation|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1996-05-23-me-7371-story.html|access-date=19 June 2015|work=Los Angeles Times|date=May 23, 1996}}</ref> As Caltech's president, Everhart authorized the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) project, a large-scale experiment that seeks to detect gravitational waves and use them for fundamental research in physics and astronomy.<ref name=CaltechHistory>{{cite web|title=History & Milestones|url=https://www.caltech.edu/content/history-milestones|website=Caltech|accessdate=19 June 2015}}</ref>

While at Caltech, Everhart was involved in substantial expansion of the university, heading a $350-million fund-raising drive. In 1989, he helped dedicate the [[Beckman Institute at Caltech]], a research center for biology, chemistry, and related sciences.<ref name=BeckmanCaltech>{{cite journal|title=Dedicating Beckman Institute|journal=Caltech News|date=1989|volume=23|issue=6|pages=1–2|url=http://caltechcampuspubs.library.caltech.edu/2440/1/1989_12_23_06.pdf|accessdate=19 June 2015}}</ref> It was the second of five research centers supported by [[Arnold Orville Beckman]] and his wife Mabel.  Everhart also was involved in the development of the [[W. M. Keck Observatory]] in Hawaii, supported by the [[W. M. Keck Foundation]];<ref name=Copman>{{cite web|last1=Copman|first1=Linda|last2=Kamisato|first2=Peggi|title=Visionary Philanthropy: A Home Run|url=http://cosmicmatters.keckobservatory.org/2007/sept/07sept_3.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110413170130/http://cosmicmatters.keckobservatory.org/2007/sept/07sept_3.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=2011-04-13|website=Cosmic Matters, Keck Observatory|date=2007}}</ref> the Gordon and Betty Moore Laboratory of Engineering, supported by [[Gordon Moore]] of [[Intel]];<ref name=Flanigan>{{cite news|last1=Flanigan|first1=James|title=With Its New Lab, Caltech Has a Formula to Survive Uncertainty|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1996-01-10-fi-22960-story.html|access-date=19 June 2015|work=Los Angeles Times|date=January 10, 1996}}</ref>  and the Fairchild Engineering Library, supported by the [[Sherman Fairchild Foundation]].<ref name=Woo/><ref name=Fairchild>{{cite web|last1=Douglas|first1=Kimberly|title=Sherman Fairchild Library: Ten Years Later|url=http://www.eas.caltech.edu/engenious/six/campus_resource|website=Division of Engineering and Applied Science|publisher=Caltech|accessdate=19 June 2015}}</ref>

Everhart promoted efforts to hire more female faculty and increase the enrollment of women. In his final year at Caltech the number of women in the freshmen class was double that of the year he joined Caltech.<ref name=Woo/>

Since 1998, Everhart has served as a trustee of the [[California Institute of Technology]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Former Caltech President Tom Everhart Elected to Board|url=https://www.caltech.edu/news/former-caltech-president-tom-everhart-elected-board-299|accessdate=19 June 2015|work=Caltech News and Events|date=1998}}</ref>  He sits on the boards of directors of [[Raytheon]] and the [[Kavli Foundation (United States)|Kavli Foundation]], among others.<ref name=Kavli>{{cite web|title=Thomas E. Everhart|url=http://www.kavlifoundation.org/thomas-e-everhart|website=The Kavli Foundation|accessdate=19 June 2015}}</ref>

=== Harvard University ===
In 1999, Everhart was elected to a six-year term as Overseer of [[Harvard University]]. In 2001 he became a member of the Overseers executive committee.  He was one of three overseers who participated in the university's presidential search committee in 2000-01.  In 2004, he was elected president of Harvard's Board of Overseers for 2004-05.<ref name=Harvard2004>{{cite news|title=Everhart named Overseers president for 2004-05|url=http://news.harvard.edu/gazette/2004/06.10/09-overseers.html|accessdate=19 June 2015|work=Harvard Gazette|date=June 10, 2004}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==
Everhart has been elected to a number of scientific societies, including the following:<ref name=OralHistoryCHF/>

* 1969, 	Fellow, [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]]
* 1977,     President, [[Electron Microscope Society of America]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://microscopy.org/past-presidents|title=MSA Past Presidents|publisher= Microscopy Society of America|accessdate= 15 April 2025}}</ref>
* 1978, 	Member, [[National Academy of Engineering]]
* 1984, 	Scientific Member, Böhmische Physical Society
* 1988, 	Fellow, [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]
* 1990, 	Foreign Member, [[Royal Academy of Engineering]]

Everhart has received a number of awards, including the following:<ref name=OralHistoryCHF/>

*1955, [[Marshall Scholarship]]
*1984, [[IEEE Centennial Medal]]
*1992, [[Clark Kerr Award]] 
*1993, ASEE Centennial Medallion
*2002, [[IEEE Founders Medal]] 
*2002, Okawa Prize
